ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The ComBaCaL cohort study and ongoing nested trials, including the present usability sub-study, were approved by the National Health Research Ethics Committee in Lesotho (ID 210-2022 and ID 210-2022 Nested).
The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Participants were additionally asked about usability, satisfaction, perceived value, ease of performing specific clinical tasks, perceived benefits and challenges of system use, and recommendations for future implementation.

Participants were selected using purposive maximum-variation sampling to capture a broad range of experiences across districts, age, sex, village accessibility, trial arm allocation, digital literacy, and previous work experience as a CHW.
Remote supervisor checking was reported to 429 increase confidence by 77 (75%) CHWs, while 75 (73%) reported greater confidence that messages 430 communicated to participants were correct.
table.header: Ease of use of general application functions and clinical tasks

table.text: Measure Community health workers (N=103), n (%) Perceived benefits Task reminders 95 (92%) Guidance for procedures and questionnaires 90 (87%) Overview of participants and tasks 83 (81%) Data saved on tablet and record retention 83 (81%) Remote supervisor checking gives confidence 77 (75%) Confidence that messages to participants are correct 75 (73%) Access to participant information 67 (65%) Other benefit 13 (13%) Perceived challenges Questionnaires too long 66 (64%) Charging the tablet difficult 50 (49%) Poor internet connection makes syncing difficult 34 (33%) Takes too much time 21 (20%) Cannot adapt tasks to own schedule 16 (16%) Too many technical problems 14 (14%) Too many tasks 13 (13%) Supervisors can check entered data 6 (6%) Data privacy concerns 5 (5%) Too complicated to use 2 (2%) Measure Community health workers (N=103), n (%) Other challenge 2 (2%) Suggested improvements Better overview of households and participants 51 (50%) SMS messages to clients 48 (47%) Fewer questions 34 (33%) More detailed information/instruction 31 (30%) Ability to schedule tasks themselves 25 (24%) Less detailed information/instruction 18 (17%) Other improvement 4 (4%) 433 SMS, short message service.
table.header: Ease of use of general application functions and clinical tasks

table.text: Operationally, some CHWs wanted greater control over task timing when participants were unavailable, suggesting that structured follow-up schedules need sufficient flexibility to accommodate circumstances outside the CHW's control.

Although SMS reminders to participants were among the most requested additions, CHWs themselves raised confidentiality and safety concerns about messaging participants on shared phones, illustrating the value of involving frontline users before adding features that may carry social risks.

Notably, the qualitative component elicited criticisms and tensions as well as positive assessments, indicating participants were willing to voice concerns and offering some reassurance against uniformly positive reporting.

Four participants had previous experience working as CHWs before the introduction of the digital system and were therefore able to reflect on differences between paper-based and digital workflows.Semi-structured interview guides explored experiences using the application, perceived benefits and challenges, training and support needs, usability, and the role of the application in supporting delivery of hypertension and diabetes care.
Participants were informed of his role and the purpose of the qualitative study before data collection.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

    Where = c("line 34, line 35", "line 2, line 5, line 6, line 7, line 8, ..."
    ), Key = c(1L, 1L), "Type of key" = c("generic-credential-uri", 
    "generic-credential-uri"), Beginning = c("pass...", "pass..."

Revoke each key with its provider and make a new one, then remove it from the files. Deleting the file or the line does not remove the key: GitHub keeps every earlier version of a repository, and the OSF keeps earlier versions of a file. Metacheck shows only the beginning of each key, and does not test whether it still works.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 359 columns across 57 data files.
#### Issues Identified

322 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 57 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

ethics_statements: The ComBaCaL cohort study and ongoing nested trials, including the present usability sub-study, were approved by the National Health Research Ethics Committee in Lesotho (ID 210-2022 and ID 210-2022 Nested).
The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: Participants were additionally asked about usability, satisfaction, perceived value, ease of performing specific clinical tasks, perceived benefits and challenges of system use, and recommendations for future implementation.

Participants were selected using purposive maximum-variation sampling to capture a broad range of experiences across districts, age, sex, village accessibility, trial arm allocation, digital literacy, and previous work experience as a CHW.
Remote supervisor checking was reported to 429 increase confidence by 77 (75%) CHWs, while 75 (73%) reported greater confidence that messages 430 communicated to participants were correct.

Measure Community health workers (N=103), n (%) Perceived benefits Task reminders 95 (92%) Guidance for procedures and questionnaires 90 (87%) Overview of participants and tasks 83 (81%) Data saved on tablet and record retention 83 (81%) Remote supervisor checking gives confidence 77 (75%) Confidence that messages to participants are correct 75 (73%) Access to participant information 67 (65%) Other benefit 13 (13%) Perceived challenges Questionnaires too long 66 (64%) Charging the tablet difficult 50 (49%) Poor internet connection makes syncing difficult 34 (33%) Takes too much time 21 (20%) Cannot adapt tasks to own schedule 16 (16%) Too many technical problems 14 (14%) Too many tasks 13 (13%) Supervisors can check entered data 6 (6%) Data privacy concerns 5 (5%) Too complicated to use 2 (2%) Measure Community health workers (N=103), n (%) Other challenge 2 (2%) Suggested improvements Better overview of households and participants 51 (50%) SMS messages to clients 48 (47%) Fewer questions 34 (33%) More detailed information/instruction 31 (30%) Ability to schedule tasks themselves 25 (24%) Less detailed information/instruction 18 (17%) Other improvement 4 (4%) 433 SMS, short message service.

Operationally, some CHWs wanted greater control over task timing when participants were unavailable, suggesting that structured follow-up schedules need sufficient flexibility to accommodate circumstances outside the CHW's control.

Although SMS reminders to participants were among the most requested additions, CHWs themselves raised confidentiality and safety concerns about messaging participants on shared phones, illustrating the value of involving frontline users before adding features that may carry social risks.

Notably, the qualitative component elicited criticisms and tensions as well as positive assessments, indicating participants were willing to voice concerns and offering some reassurance against uniformly positive reporting.

Four participants had previous experience working as CHWs before the introduction of the digital system and were therefore able to reflect on differences between paper-based and digital workflows.Semi-structured interview guides explored experiences using the application, perceived benefits and challenges, training and support needs, usability, and the role of the application in supporting delivery of hypertension and diabetes care.
Participants were informed of his role and the purpose of the qualitative study before data collection.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.

report: ### Python code
This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 Python code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()`-equivalent, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:7, File = c("BPForm.py", "createDataGroupAnyFormToAnyForms.py", 
"createDataGroupBPFormToBPForm.py", "createTranslationsFromForm.py", 
"editBPForms.py", "editDMForms.py", "extractVillages.py"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("none", 
"none", "none", "none", "none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files not run on their own
1 file is empty, so there is nothing to run, and it is not counted as a script: BPForm.py.
#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("BPForm.py", "createDataGroupAnyFormToAnyForms.py", 
"createDataGroupBPFormToBPForm.py", "createTranslationsFromForm.py", 
"editBPForms.py", "editDMForms.py", "extractVillages.py"), Outcome = c("empty", 
"needs_a_person", "needs_a_person", "ran_ok", "needs_a_person", 
"needs_a_person", "needs_a_person"), Detail = c("", "EOFError", 
"EOFError", "", "EOFError", "EOFError", "EOFError"), "Time (s)" = c(0, 
1.5, 0.8, 19.7, 0.6, 0.6, 1)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```

text.text: Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly delivering chronic care in resource-constrained settings but require support to manage complex longitudinal clinical workflows.

In the Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project in rural Lesotho, CHWs provide longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care, supported by the ComBaCaL Community Health Toolkit (CHT) application.

The application combines longitudinal participant management and task coordination with clinical decision support for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, and follow-up for hypertension and diabetes care.
This model of care has demonstrated improved or maintained clinical outcomes compared to facility-based care only.
We conducted a mixed-methods study among all 103 participating CHWs to evaluate their experiences with the application.
All CHWs completed a 38-item questionnaire, and 22 participated in qualitative interviews or focus group discussions.
Overall usability was high, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 75.6 (SD 13.0), and 98 (95%) CHWs were satisfied or very satisfied with the application.
General application functions and diagnosis and treatment tasks were rated easy or very easy by 98% of participants.
The most frequently reported benefits were task reminders (92%), structured clinical guidance (87%), overview of allocated participants (81%), and retention of participant information (81%).
Main challenges were lengthy questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, and limited internet connectivity.
Qualitative findings showed that ease of use increased with experience, supported by training and supervision.
Participants described how algorithmic guidance and task reminders supported care delivery, while also identifying tensions between standardized workflows and flexibility in day-to-day care.
The ComBaCaL CHT application was highly usable and valued by CHWs.
High perceived usability extended from general application functions to complex clinical workflows.

CHT demonstrated suitability as a configurable framework for implementing such context-specific workflows for hypertension and diabetes care when accompanied by appropriate workflow design, training, and supervision.
High blood pressure and diabetes require repeated follow-up and treatment decisions, which is difficult where healthcare professionals are scarce.
Community health workers (CHWs) may help expand access to this care, but they need appropriate tools to manage complex clinical tasks.
We evaluated a digital application designed to support CHWs in delivering hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho.
Overall, 103 CHWs used an application built with the Community Health Toolkit to support hypertension and diabetes care.
The application helped manage participants and follow-up tasks and provided stepby-step guidance for screening, diagnosis, treatment, referral, and repeated care visits.
All 103 CHWs completed a survey, and 22 participated in interviews or focus group discussions.
CHWs found the application easy to use and useful for their work.
Frequently reported benefits included reminders, procedural guidance, better participant oversight, and retention of participant information over time.
Ease of use improved with experience and was supported by training and supervision.
Challenges included lengthy research questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, limited internet connectivity, and standardized digital workflows that did not fit day-to-day circumstances.
Our findings show that a configurable open-source digital application can support CHWs in delivering complex, longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in a remote rural setting.

Task-shifting to lay health providers such as community health workers (CHWs) has emerged as a promising strategy to improve access to essential health services in resource-constrained settings [1, 2].
text.formatted: Task-shifting to lay health providers such as community health workers (CHWs) has emerged as a promising strategy to improve access to essential health services in resource-constrained settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: CHWs are trained members of their communities and can help overcome barriers related to travel distance, costs, and healthcare workforce shortages.

While CHW-led healthcare delivery models have demonstrated effectiveness for health promotion, screening, and linkage to care, their role in longitudinal management of chronic diseases, such as hypertension and type 2 diabetes, remains limited [3, 4].
text.formatted: While CHW-led healthcare delivery models have demonstrated effectiveness for health promotion, screening, and linkage to care, their role in longitudinal management of chronic diseases, such as hypertension and type 2 diabetes, remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Hypertension and type 2 diabetes are among the leading contributors to morbidity and mortality in lowand middle-income countries, yet gaps in diagnosis, treatment, and long-term control persist, particularly in rural areas [5] [6] [7].
text.formatted: Hypertension and type 2 diabetes are among the leading contributors to morbidity and mortality in lowand middle-income countries, yet gaps in diagnosis, treatment, and long-term control persist, particularly in rural areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Shortages of trained healthcare professionals, geographic barriers to care, and limited health system resources continue to constrain access to care for these conditions [8].
text.formatted: Shortages of trained healthcare professionals, geographic barriers to care, and limited health system resources continue to constrain access to care for these conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Their management requires repeated assessments, treatment decisions, medication management, and long-term follow-up, activities that have traditionally been performed by more highly trained healthcare professionals.
Expanding the role of CHWs to include these tasks therefore requires approaches that ensure care remains safe, consistent, and aligned with clinical guidelines.
Digital clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) have been proposed to extend the scope and quality of community-based healthcare delivery [9].
text.formatted: Digital clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) have been proposed to extend the scope and quality of community-based healthcare delivery <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: By guiding users through standardized workflows, supporting clinical decision-making, and enabling remote supervision, digital tools may help address some of the operational and clinical challenges associated with task-shifted care [10].
text.formatted: By guiding users through standardized workflows, supporting clinical decision-making, and enabling remote supervision, digital tools may help address some of the operational and clinical challenges associated with task-shifted care <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, many community health programs continue to rely on fragmented or paper-based information systems, making it difficult to maintain longitudinal patient records, coordinate follow-up, and provide effective supervision [11].
text.formatted: Additionally, many community health programs continue to rely on fragmented or paper-based information systems, making it difficult to maintain longitudinal patient records, coordinate follow-up, and provide effective supervision <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Digital platforms that combine longitudinal data capture with clinical decision support could thus support both continuity of care and program oversight.
However, evidence on how CHWs experience and use digital systems that support complex care processes, including diagnosis, treatment initiation, titration and long-term follow-up remains limited.
Many digital health interventions are developed as stand-alone applications with limited interoperability, scalability, and long-term sustainability [12].
text.formatted: Many digital health interventions are developed as stand-alone applications with limited interoperability, scalability, and long-term sustainability <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Increasing attention is therefore being directed toward digital public goods and open-source platforms that can be adapted to local contexts while supporting integration into routine health systems [13].
text.formatted: Increasing attention is therefore being directed toward digital public goods and open-source platforms that can be adapted to local contexts while supporting integration into routine health systems <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref>.

text.text: The Community Health Toolkit (CHT) is an established open-source framework for developing configurable digital health applications for community health systems.
Its core framework provides a common user interface that can be customized to support different health system hierarchies, roles, and program needs.

Designed as an offline-first tool, CHT supports longitudinal patient and household records, care guides for healthworker decision support, tasks to ensure timely care, in-app dashboards for performance management, and messaging for rapid communication [14].
text.formatted: Designed as an offline-first tool, CHT supports longitudinal patient and household records, care guides for healthworker decision support, tasks to ensure timely care, in-app dashboards for performance management, and messaging for rapid communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[14]</ref>.

text.text: CHT-based applications have been implemented across diverse health programs and on a national scale in several countries.

Previous studies of CHT-based applications have demonstrated usability and acceptability for more focused workflows, including twoway communication and follow-up after voluntary medical male circumcision and for retention in HIV care [15, 16].
text.formatted: Previous studies of CHT-based applications have demonstrated usability and acceptability for more focused workflows, including twoway communication and follow-up after voluntary medical male circumcision and for retention in HIV care <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">16]</ref>.

text.text: Evidence remains limited, however, on the use of CHT to support the complex, longitudinal management of hypertension and type 2 diabetes by lay CHWs.
The Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project was established in rural Lesotho to develop and evaluate innovative models of community-based chronic care [17].
text.formatted: The Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project was established in rural Lesotho to develop and evaluate innovative models of community-based chronic care <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Within the project, a mobile application based on the CHT framework was developed to support longitudinal populationbased data collection alongside screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation, medication management, and longitudinal follow-up of individuals with hypertension and type 2 diabetes (ComBaCaL CHT application) [18] [19] [20].
text.formatted: Within the project, a mobile application based on the CHT framework was developed to support longitudinal populationbased data collection alongside screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation, medication management, and longitudinal follow-up of individuals with hypertension and type 2 diabetes (ComBaCaL CHT application) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[20]</ref>.

text.text: The feasibility and acceptability of the approach were first assessed in a pilot study conducted in ten villages with one CHW each [21] [22] [23].
text.formatted: The feasibility and acceptability of the approach were first assessed in a pilot study conducted in ten villages with one CHW each <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Lessons learned during this pilot informed further refinement of the application and its workflows, most notably the consolidation of separate screening, treatmentinitiation, and follow-up forms into a single, adaptive form that adjusts to each participant's current . diagnostic and treatment status, accommodating any care state encountered over repeated visits.

The resulting system was subsequently implemented by 103 CHWs across 103 rural villages and formed a core component of three cluster-randomized trials evaluating CHW-led hypertension and diabetes care [18, 19].
text.formatted: The resulting system was subsequently implemented by 103 CHWs across 103 rural villages and formed a core component of three cluster-randomized trials evaluating CHW-led hypertension and diabetes care <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">19]</ref>.

text.text: These trials demonstrated improved hypertension control among individuals with uncontrolled hypertension, improved engagement in care among individuals with type 2 diabetes, and non-inferior outcomes among individuals with controlled hypertension receiving the additional option of CHW-led compared with facility-based nurse-led care alone [24] [25] [26].
text.formatted: These trials demonstrated improved hypertension control among individuals with uncontrolled hypertension, improved engagement in care among individuals with type 2 diabetes, and non-inferior outcomes among individuals with controlled hypertension receiving the additional option of CHW-led compared with facility-based nurse-led care alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[26]</ref>.

text.text: While the previous studies examined the initial feasibility and design of the digital approach and subsequent trials established the effectiveness of the broader care models, the usability of the mature application and CHWs' experiences using it for longitudinal care have not been comprehensively evaluated.
Understanding how frontline health workers experience digital CDSSs is essential for informing future scale-up and adaptation of community-based care models [27].
text.formatted: Understanding how frontline health workers experience digital CDSSs is essential for informing future scale-up and adaptation of community-based care models <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[27]</ref>.

text.text: We therefore describe the design and implementation of the ComBaCaL CHT application and report a mixed-methods evaluation among all 103 CHWs using the system.

We aimed to assess its usability, user satisfaction, and perceived value and to explore how CHWs experienced the use of the platform to support complex longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in remote rural communities.

The ComBaCaL project is a community-based research and service delivery platform established by a consortium including the Lesotho Ministry of Health, local community representatives, the local nonprofit organization SolidarMed and the University of Basel, Switzerland, in the rural districts of Butha-Buthe and Mokhotlong, Lesotho.
Its core component is a population-based cohort comprising 103 villages with one participating CHW per village.

Villages were selected independently of CHW characteristics; where no active CHW was available, a new CHW was elected by the village population in collaboration with the Ministry of Health according to national procedures [28].
text.formatted: Villages were selected independently of CHW characteristics; where no active CHW was available, a new CHW was elected by the village population in collaboration with the Ministry of Health according to national procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[28]</ref>.

text.text: The cohort serves as a platform for the evaluation of community-based care models through embedded cluster-randomized trials and implementation studies.
At the time of this evaluation, the primary analysis of three clusterrandomized trials assessing CHW-led hypertension and diabetes care had been completed [24] [25] [26].
text.formatted: At the time of this evaluation, the primary analysis of three clusterrandomized trials assessing CHW-led hypertension and diabetes care had been completed <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[26]</ref>.

text.text: All CHWs were provided with Android tablets (Lenovo TabM10 FHD Plus Model TB-X606X) with the ComBaCaL CHT application installed and with power banks; CHWs in selected villages with limited access to electricity additionally received portable solar charging systems.
After cohort enrollment and baseline data collection, all CHWs conducted community-based screening and diagnosis of hypertension and type 2 diabetes.

In 51 of 103 villages allocated to the intervention arms of the nested trials, CHWs additionally deliver protocol-based treatment and follow-up of eligible participants with hypertension and/or type 2 diabetes.
CHWs received structured initial training on the clinical protocols and the application over roughly 10 days, followed by short refresher trainings at roughly 6-month intervals.

During implementation, they received clinical support from routine facilitybased nursing staff during regular monthly meetings and by study staff who reviewed submitted records and program-monitoring dashboards through the web-based interface and provided clinical and operational feedback.
Technical support for devices, connectivity, and application issues was provided by the ComBaCaL study team through phone calls or village visits if needed.
Details of the ComBaCaL cohort, trial designs, intervention protocols and consent procedures have been published previously [17] [18] [19] [20] [24] [25] [26].
text.formatted: Details of the ComBaCaL cohort, trial designs, intervention protocols and consent procedures have been published previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[26]</ref>.

text.text: To support longitudinal population-based data collection and community-based hypertension and diabetes care, we developed the ComBaCaL application (hereafter referred to as "the application") using the open-source CHT Core Framework (versions 3.12, 3.14, 4.6, and 4.13), available at https://github.com/clinepi-usb/cht-combacal.
text.formatted: To support longitudinal population-based data collection and community-based hypertension and diabetes care, we developed the ComBaCaL application (hereafter referred to as "the application") using the open-source CHT Core Framework (versions 3.12, 3.14, 4.6, and 4.13), available at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/clinepi-usb/cht-combacal">https://github.com/clinepi-usb/cht-combacal</ref>.

text.text: The CHT Core Framework provided the common user interface and underlying architecture for user roles and hierarchies, household and participant records, longitudinal participant profiles, task management, reporting, program monitoring, participant search, and offline data storage and synchronization.
Within this framework, we configured the ComBaCaLspecific forms, task rules, research and cohort workflows, translations, and clinical decision support for hypertension and diabetes care.
The CDSS component provided protocol-based guidance for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, counseling, and longitudinal follow-up.

A messaging component available within the CHT Core Framework was not implemented because it was not a key project requirement and integration with local short message service (SMS) infrastructure proved technically challenging.
The platform further supports role-based access through configurable user hierarchies.

CHWs access the application on the password-protected tablets, while supervisors access the same system through a web-based interface that allows review of participant records, submitted reports, and program monitoring information across all villages under their supervision.
Data were stored locally on the tablets for offline use and synchronized when connectivity was available to secure servers hosted at the University Hospital Basel, Switzerland.
Routine health-facility staff continued to use existing facility-based documentation and reporting systems.

Although CHT supports interoperability with other complementary health-information systems, direct electronic integration with the national reporting architecture was outside the scope of this initial research implementation.

To maintain alignment with established Ministry of Health reporting pathways, CHWs reported relevant activities to supervising facility staff for entry into routine facility registers rather than replacing the existing reporting architecture with direct digital reporting from the application.
The application workflow begins with household registration followed by registration of individual household members.
After informed consent and baseline data collection, participants become eligible for hypertension and type 2 diabetes screening according to predefined criteria.
Screening and diagnosis followed the Lesotho Standard Treatment Guidelines with confirmation of elevated blood pressure or blood glucose required on two different visits for a diagnosis [29].
text.formatted: Screening and diagnosis followed the Lesotho Standard Treatment Guidelines with confirmation of elevated blood pressure or blood glucose required on two different visits for a diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Participants remained within a longitudinal record that was updated during subsequent encounters, with previous and current clinical information used to determine subsequent assessments and care.
Full screening and diagnostic algorithms are provided in the Supporting Information (S1 and S2 Figs).

During screening and follow-up, CHWs collected information on medication use, comorbidities, symptoms, blood pressure, blood glucose, and other clinical information required to determine the participant's current care status.
In intervention villages, the CDSS component additionally guided protocol-based treatment and follow-up.

This included lifestyle counseling, initiation, titration and deescalation of first-line pharmacological treatment (amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide combination pill for hypertension; metformin for type 2 diabetes), cardiovascular risk-based preventive treatment (atorvastatin and aspirin according to predefined eligibility criteria), referral, and follow-up scheduling.
In control villages, CHWs provided lifestyle counseling and referral to facility-based care.
Full treatment algorithms are provided in the Supporting Information (S3 and S4 Figs).
Unlike its pilot version, which used separate forms for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation, and follow-up, the final application is designed as a longitudinal, adaptive workflow [21, 22].

text.text: This redesign was necessary because participants frequently transition between different care states over time, making linear screening-to-treatment workflows insufficient for routine chronic disease care.
The application integrates information from previous visits and current assessments to determine a participant's care status and dynamically guide the CHW through the next appropriate action (Fig 1).

text.text: This design allows a single workflow to support the full continuum of community-based chronic disease care while accommodating changes in clinical circumstances, participant preferences, treatment uptake, equipment availability, medication availability, and other factors encountered during routine care.
We conducted a mixed-methods study to evaluate CHWs' experiences using the application.

The study combined a quantitative survey administered to all participating CHWs with qualitative individual indepth interviews (IDIs) and focus group discussions (FGDs) among a purposively selected subset of CHWs.
Quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed separately and subsequently integrated during interpretation.
All 103 CHWs participating in the ComBaCaL project were invited to complete a structured 38-item survey.
The survey collected information on demographic characteristics, education level, English proficiency, and prior digital experience.

Participants were additionally asked about usability, satisfaction, perceived value, ease of performing specific clinical tasks, perceived benefits and challenges of system use, and recommendations for future implementation.

Usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), a validated ten-item questionnaire consisting of alternating positive and negative statements rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree [30].
text.formatted: Usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), a validated ten-item questionnaire consisting of alternating positive and negative statements rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Responses were converted into a composite score ranging from 0 to 100 according to standard scoring procedures, with higher scores indicating greater perceived usability.
Additional survey items were adapted from established instruments and tailored to the ComBaCaL context.

Items assessing perceived usefulness, communication, interface, and overall satisfaction were adapted from the mHealth App Usability Questionnaire (MAUQ) [31], while selected items on perceived effects on care delivery and clinical decision-making were adapted from the Primary Care Information Project Provider Survey [32].

Survey questions and answer choices were presented in both English and the local language, Sesotho.

To obtain an in-depth understanding of CHWs' experiences using the application, we conducted semistructured IDIs and FGDs.

Participants were selected using purposive maximum-variation sampling to capture a broad range of experiences across districts, age, sex, village accessibility, trial arm allocation, digital literacy, and previous work experience as a CHW.

The qualitative sample size was determined a priori through purposive maximum-variation sampling, with the option to conduct additional interviews had the predefined sample not proven sufficiently rich; the sampled range was judged to provide comprehensive accounts, and no further interviews were required.
Selected CHWs were invited faceto-face during a regular clinical training, and all invited participants agreed to participate.

Qualitative data were analyzed using framework analysis.

An initial analytical framework was informed by domains covered in the quantitative survey and semi-structured interview guide, including usability and perceived value, ease of use of general application functions and clinical tasks, and perceived benefits, challenges, and opportunities for improvement.
Coding combined deductive application of these predefined domains with inductive identification of additional codes arising from the data.
Two researchers (AA, FG) conducted the analysis collaboratively and iteratively.
An initial coding framework and analysis matrix were developed, compared across transcripts, discussed, and refined until agreement was reached.

Codes and categories were further refined through comparison across participants and data sources and organized into four overarching themes: (1) usability, learning, and enabling conditions; (2) how the application supported longitudinal chronic care; (3) challenges and tensions; and (4) suggested adaptations and future development.
Findings extending beyond the predefined survey domains were retained within the analytical framework.
Coding and matrix development were performed manually.

text.text: We used a convergent mixed-methods design in which quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed separately and integrated during interpretation and reporting.

Because the qualitative interview guides covered domains also assessed in the survey, the two data sources addressed overlapping aspects of usability, clinical task support, perceived benefits, and implementation challenges.

During integration, qualitative findings were compared with the corresponding survey results to identify areas of convergence, divergence, and additional insights not captured by the predefined survey items.
Qualitative findings were used both to contextualize quantitative results and to explore mechanisms through which the application supported hypertension and diabetes care.
Reporting of the mixedmethods design follows the Good Reporting of A Mixed Methods Study (GRAMMS) criteria [37]; the completed checklist is provided in the Supporting Information (S2 Checklist).

text.text: The Ministry of Health of Lesotho and the District Management Teams of Butha-Buthe district were among the initial members of the research consortium.
Community-engaged research is key in the ComBaCaL project.
The CHWs are members of the community and have been elected by the community.
Research questions for nested trials are based on feedback from community-members during implementation of the ComBaCaL activities.
Prior to implementation of the ComBaCaL cohort, we conducted a pilot study to incorporate views and perceptions of the local community and CHWs in the final design of the study and nested trials.
Community representatives will be involved in the development of protocols for further nested trials.

At the SUS item level ( S2 Table), responses were strongly favorable for frequent use, integration, and confidence: 98% would like to use the application frequently, 96% found its functions well integrated, and 96% felt confident using it, while most disagreed that it was complex (83%) or awkward to use (85%).

text.text: Responses were more mixed on the learnability items: while 74% expected most CHWs to learn the application quickly, a majority reported needing to learn a lot of things before getting started (61%) and 31% reported potentially needing technical support.
Only 32% responded favorably to the item on perceived inconsistency, compared with 96% who reported that the application's functions were well integrated.
The qualitative data contextualized these findings by showing that ease of use developed with experience.
Participants described initial difficulty during training and early use, followed by increasing familiarity with the application:
When I first used CHT I thought it was a lot during the training when we were practicing, but as I was using it, it became easy.
Although it gets easy with time, you still forget other things, therefore you need to keep reminding yourself all the time like today at the refreshers."

(IDI, female CHW, Butha-Buthe) This trajectory extended to CHWs with no prior smartphone experience, consistent with the expectation that most would learn the application quickly: "It was my first time using a smartphone, it was so difficult to navigate.
But now it's easy."

(FGD, Mokhotlong) Other participants similarly described practice during training and access to supervisors as helping them become comfortable with the system, while noting that some CHWs continued to require additional training.
The bilingual English/Sesotho design was also described as facilitating use and supporting the application's fit with CHWs' work.
At the same time, participants raised concerns about whether the same experience would extend to the wider CHW workforce, particularly older or less educated CHWs with limited digital experience.
One CHW explained: "It could be useful but those CHWs are old people most of them and did not really go far in terms of education.
It might be really complicated to train them to use CHT."
(IDI, male CHW, Butha-Buthe) This concern was not universal: other participants considered such barriers potentially manageable with adequate training and support.
CHWs reported that both the core application functions and clinical tasks were easy to perform using the application (Table 3).
text.formatted: CHWs reported that both the core application functions and clinical tasks were easy to perform using the application (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: Registering households and participants, keeping track of pending tasks, and reviewing submitted reports were rated easy or very easy by almost all participants (94-97%), as were diagnosis of hypertension and type 2 diabetes (98%) and giving correct treatment advice (94%).

The application was also seen as adding value to clinical work: 66 (64%) CHWs reported that diagnosing hypertension and diabetes without it would be more difficult, and 38 of 51 (75%) intervention CHWs reported that providing hypertension and type 2 diabetes treatment would be more difficult without the application.

434 435 Qualitative findings illustrated how these benefits supported day-to-day work.

Participants described 436 task reminders as helping them plan upcoming visits and prepare required medicines and other 437 commodities, while longitudinal participant records facilitated access to information from previous 438 encounters and reduced reliance on paper records that could be lost.
Participants also linked the clinical 439 guidance provided by the application to greater confidence and credibility with patients.

Beyond these 440 direct functions, some described digital documentation as strengthening accountability by making 441 completed work traceable: 442 "Without CHT I think our work would lack credibility, there was going to be a lot of cheating but with 443 CHT there is no chance of cheating."
(FGD, Butha-Buthe) 444 Another participant similarly contrasted the application with paper-based reporting, where tasks could 445 be recorded as completed without necessarily having been performed.

While supervisory visibility was 446 frequently perceived positively, 6 (6%) CHWs identified supervisors being able to check entered data as 447 a challenge and 5 (5%) reported data-privacy concerns (Table 4).

text.text: Qualitative accounts also showed that 448 task visibility could have unintended consequences when completion depended on participant availability: one participant noted that tasks remaining pending could make it appear that the CHW was not doing the work.
The most frequently reported challenges were long questionnaires (64%), difficulty charging tablets (49%), and limited internet connectivity (33%).
Qualitative accounts indicated that much of the questionnaire burden related to research-specific consent and baseline data collection rather than the clinical care workflows themselves.
Some participants described these questions as lengthy or intrusive.
Charging difficulties were particularly relevant in villages without electricity, while poor network connectivity primarily affected synchronization.

Participants also described occasional tensions between following standardized decision support and responding to situations in which the application's recommendation did not align with their expectations or with care provided elsewhere.
That causes a lot of confusion because as a person you would also want to work the way you were trained.
But at the end of the day CHT forces you to do what it says."
(IDI, female CHW, Butha-Buthe) The participant clarified that this did not occur often but described situations in which the algorithm's recommendation differed from subsequent facility treatment.
A related tension arose when the algorithm recommended reducing or discontinuing antihypertensive medication.

Participants described difficulty explaining this to patients who understood antihypertensive treatment to be lifelong: "...some of the patients do not trust what we say to them because they have an old information that when you are on this kind of treatment you are not to stop taking medication."
(FGD, Mokhotlong)
The same participant suggested that confirmation from a facility nurse could help patients accept such treatment changes.

In one interview, a CHW also described having become reliant on the application's confirmation when diagnosing hypertension and type 2 diabetes, illustrating that decision support could increase confidence while potentially creating dependence on the system.
Participants also identified challenges related to information continuity across care providers.

They described patients using multiple personal health booklets, treatment changes made at health facilities that were not always known to the CHW, and medication obtained from multiple sources, creating a potential risk of duplication.
"A challenge of clients who mix pills or overdose because they will be taking medication from me and when the outreach is there, they also go there and get medication."

(FGD, Butha-Buthe) Suggested improvements included a better overview of households and participants (50%), automated SMS reminders for participants (47%), fewer questions (33%), and greater flexibility in scheduling tasks (24%).

The qualitative findings supported the desire for greater scheduling flexibility: participants valued automated task reminders but described situations in which predefined task timing did not align with participant availability, and some suggested being able to schedule their own visits while retaining supervisory visibility.
Although SMS reminders were among the most requested additions, qualitative accounts revealed divergent views.

Some participants considered SMS useful for reminding participants of upcoming visits, whereas others raised concerns about limited phone ownership, low literacy, confidentiality on shared phones, and potential family conflict or safety concerns: "Most of our patients don't have phones, they share phones.
Imagine now sending a text message, it is going to raise a lot of suspicions."
(FGD, Mokhotlong)
The broader discussion in the same FGD included concerns about disclosure of illness to family members and potential conflict arising from messages sent between CHWs and participants.
One interview participant suggested telephone calls as a preferable alternative for some participants.

Additional suggestions arising from the qualitative data included enabling consultation with supervisors directly within the application, extending digital workflows to health facilities and routine Ministry of Health reporting, and broadening the platform to additional community health services such as HIV testing and family planning.

In this mixed-methods evaluation among all 103 CHWs delivering community-based hypertension and type 2 diabetes care in rural Lesotho, the ComBaCaL application was highly usable and valued by its users.

CHWs rated both the general application functions, such as participant registration and overview, task management and reporting, and the more demanding clinical tasks of diagnosis and treatment as easy, while most reported these would be harder to perform without the application.

The qualitative findings extended the survey results: usability developed through experience and was sustained by training and supervision, and CHWs described tensions around standardization, operational flexibility, accountability, and continuity of care between community and facility levels.

Together with the three nested cluster-randomized trials, which provided clinical evidence for the broader CHW-led care models, this study provides an additional, user-centered account of how the underlying application was experienced [24] [25] [26].

text.text: The ComBaCaL model extends this experience by enabling CHWs themselves to deliver the full longitudinal pathway at community level -diagnosis, independent treatment initiation and titration, cardiovascular risk management, referral and repeated follow-up.
The good overall usability, reflected in a mean SUS score of 75.6, above the commonly cited benchmark of 68 [30], is notable given the clinical and longitudinal complexity of the application.

text.text: The common interface, longitudinal records, task management, and offline-first architecture were provided by the established CHT Core Framework, while ComBaCaL-specific workflows and clinical decision support were configured within it.

The observed usability therefore reflects the combination of the underlying framework, application configuration, and the training and supervision provided, consistent with evidence that enabling conditions are important for health workers' adoption of digital technologies in low-and middle-income settings [44].

text.text: At the item level, responses were strongly favorable for integration and confidence, while learnability items were more mixed, corresponding with qualitative accounts of initial difficulty followed by increasing confidence with practice.

Responses to the single reverse-worded item on inconsistency were a notable exception: only a minority responded favorably, despite near-universal agreement that the application's functions were well integrated.
This most likely reflects variable interpretation due to lack of a specific term in Sesotho rather than genuinely inconsistent performance.
The use of CHT is also relevant to the potential for wider implementation.

Rather than developing a stand-alone application specifically for this project, the ComBaCaL workflows were configured within an open-source framework designed for reuse and large-scale deployment and already used in large-scale and national community health programs in multiple countries [14].
text.formatted: Rather than developing a stand-alone application specifically for this project, the ComBaCaL workflows were configured within an open-source framework designed for reuse and large-scale deployment and already used in large-scale and national community health programs in multiple countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[14]</ref>.

text.text: This does not establish the scalability or sustainability of the ComBaCaL application itself, but it provides an established technical foundation on which the application can be adapted and extended without rebuilding the underlying architecture.
Beyond overall usability, the findings illustrate how the application supported the longitudinal demands of chronic care.

Most CHWs reported that diagnosis and treatment would be more difficult without the application, and qualitative accounts linked this support to step-by-step guidance, safeguards, access to information from previous encounters, and task reminders.

The workflow carried information forward between visits and adapted the next recommended action as clinical status, treatment uptake, medication availability, participant preferences, or referral needs changed over time.
This allowed screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up to be managed within a single longitudinal pathway.

Taken together, the findings suggest that this degree of clinical and longitudinal complexity remained manageable for CHWs, while the study cannot isolate the application's contribution from training, supervision, medication supply, and other components of the care model.
The strongly positive assessments were accompanied by tensions between standardization and flexibility.

Operationally, some CHWs wanted greater control over task timing when participants were unavailable, suggesting that structured follow-up schedules need sufficient flexibility to accommodate circumstances outside the CHW's control.
Clinically, however, standardization remained important, particularly because CHWs were undertaking tasks such as treatment initiation and adjustment.

Participants occasionally described recommendations that were difficult to reconcile with care provided elsewhere or with patients' expectations, particularly when protocol-defined blood-pressure thresholds led to reduction or discontinuation of antihypertensive treatment.

These accounts highlight the importance of clear communication across providers, accessible supervision and escalation pathways, and training for CHWs in explaining guideline-based treatment decisions to patients.

One participant also reflected on becoming reliant on the application's confirmation when making decisions; although a single account, it underlines the importance of maintaining CHWs' clinical knowledge and supervisory support alongside digital guidance, so that decision support augments rather than replaces clinical judgment.
A further theme was accountability.

Some participants described the application as lending credibility to their work with patients and colleagues and as ensuring scheduled tasks were genuinely carried out rather than only recorded as complete, suggesting digital decision support may strengthen not only the consistency of care but also its perceived legitimacy and supervision.

This visibility was not universally welcomed: a minority saw supervisory oversight as a drawback (6%) or raised data-privacy concerns (5%), and one participant noted that tasks left pending because a participant could not be reached might make it appear the CHW had not worked.
Digital traceability can thus strengthen supervision, but performance monitoring must distinguish non-completion attributable to the CHW from tasks unresolved for reasons beyond their control.
Several practical challenges are relevant for wider implementation.

The most frequently reported challenge of lengthy questionnaires was attributed qualitatively to research-specific consent and baseline data collection rather than the clinical workflows, so the burden seen here likely overstates that of a platform used primarily for routine care.
Charging and intermittent connectivity remained relevant despite offline-first functionality.

Although SMS reminders to participants were among the most requested additions, CHWs themselves raised confidentiality and safety concerns about messaging participants on shared phones, illustrating the value of involving frontline users before adding features that may carry social risks.

More broadly, these experiences underscore the value of involving frontline CHWs in the ongoing development and adaptation of routine decision-support tools for noncommunicable diseases in Lesotho, so that usability and contextual challenges are addressed before wider rollout.
Information continuity across care providers emerged as an additional challenge.

Participants described treatment changes that were not always known to CHWs and medication obtained from multiple sources, which could complicate medication reconciliation and create a risk of duplication.

These challenges are not specific to the application and would not be fully resolved by digital integration alone, as information on care received elsewhere may remain incomplete and clinical history-taking also relies on patient-reported information.

Nevertheless, extending digital workflows across community and facility levels could improve access to shared longitudinal information and reduce avoidable gaps in communication and parallel documentation.
The study has several strengths.

All 103 CHWs completed the survey, giving complete coverage and minimizing non-response bias, and the mixed-methods design allowed survey findings to be contextualized and, at times, challenged by qualitative accounts.

Notably, the qualitative component elicited criticisms and tensions as well as positive assessments, indicating participants were willing to voice concerns and offering some reassurance against uniformly positive reporting.

The evaluation also followed sustained use across 103 villages and three cluster-randomized trials, reflecting repeated field use of a mature application rather than first impressions from a small pilot.
Several limitations apply.
The study was conducted within a single research implementation in rural Lesotho, which may limit transferability.
Participating CHWs were relatively young and probably more educated than the current national workforce.

However, villages were selected independently of CHW characteristics, and replacement CHWs were identified according to Ministry of Health procedures rather than preferentially selected for digital skills.
Participants themselves questioned whether older or less-educated CHWs would find the application as usable, and usability may differ in settings with less training, supervision, or infrastructure.

Social-desirability bias may have inflated favorable responses, as participants knew the study team had developed the application, although IDIs and FGDs were conducted by a researcher not involved in delivery and the data included criticism.

Some survey items used predefined categories that may not capture all experiences; the study assessed perceptions rather than objective performance or diagnostic accuracy and cannot isolate the application's independent contribution to the trial outcomes.
Finally, we did not evaluate the scalability or long-term sustainability of the application itself; the arrangements that routine implementation at scale would require are discussed above.

The ComBaCaL application was highly usable and valued by CHWs delivering longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho, with usability extending from general application functions to complex clinical workflows spanning diagnosis, treatment, medication management and repeated follow-up.

This supports the suitability of the open-source CHT Core Framework for complex longitudinal chronic-care applications in this setting and suggests that, with appropriate workflow design, training, supervision and infrastructure, digital decision support can help CHWs deliver guideline-based chronic care.

With the clinical evidence from the ComBaCaL trials, these findings support digitally enabled community-based chronic care, including independent first-line medication management, while identifying operational flexibility and integration across health-system levels as priorities for wider implementation.

text.text: Item-level responses to the System Usability Scale.
Distribution of responses to each of the ten System Usability Scale (SUS) items among all 103 community health workers.

Odd-numbered items are positively worded and even-numbered items are negatively worded; favorable responses correspond to agreement with positively worded items and disagreement with negatively worded items.
For each item, the proportion of favorable responses is shown alongside the full distribution across the five-point Likert scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree).
Full quantitative survey administered to all 103 community health workers, presented in both English and Sesotho.

The instrument covers demographic characteristics, educational attainment, English proficiency, and prior digital experience; the System Usability Scale; items on perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and perceived value adapted from the mHealth App Usability Questionnaire (MAUQ) and the Primary Care Information Project Provider Survey; task-specific ease-of-use items adapted from the Single Ease Question approach; and study-specific items on perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations for future implementation.

FBG: fasting blood glucose; RBG: random blood glucose.
Capillary blood was used for all measurements.
Measurements were considered fasting blood glucose if participants reported no caloric intake in the eight hours before the measurement; all other measurements were considered random blood glucose.

Type 2 diabetes was defined as (1) self-reported use of antidiabetic medication; (2) an FBG ≥ 7 mmol/l or an RBG ≥ 11.1 mmol/l after a previously elevated FBG or RBG ≥ 5.6 mmol/l; or (3) an FBG ≥ 7 mmol/l or an RBG ≥ 11.1 mmol/l in the presence of all three cardinal symptoms of uncontrolled diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss) in the absence of a clinical history suggestive of type 1 diabetes.

text.text: At every visit, the community health worker (CHW) documented current medication, adherence, and blood pressure values.
Measurements were taken after selecting the appropriate cuff size, with participants seated after at least five minutes of rest.
At the initial visit, blood pressure was measured in both arms, and subsequent measurements were taken from the arm with the higher systolic pressure.
The blood pressure value was calculated as the mean of the last two of three consecutive measurements obtained at one-minute intervals.

If no contraindications were present, CHWs offered a fixed-dose combination pill containing amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide, with titration according to the algorithm of the Lesotho Standard Treatment Guidelines.

Participants with a blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg under highdose amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide, those with contraindications or intolerance to amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide, and those refusing the medications offered by the CHW were referred to the closest health facility.
Treatment was discontinued or de-intensified if systolic blood pressure was < 120 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure was < 90 mmHg.
text.formatted: Treatment was discontinued or de-intensified if systolic blood pressure was < 120 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure was < 90 mmHg.

text.text: Follow-up visits were scheduled after one month if the dose was adjusted during the index visit, or after two months if the dose was not adjusted.
Participants with high CVD risk and no contraindications were offered atorvastatin 10 mg daily.

High CVD risk among people with hypertension was defined as a history of stroke or myocardial infarction; diabetes or chronic kidney disease; or being ≥ 50 years old and currently smoking or having a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m².
Participants with a history of myocardial infarction or stroke were offered acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) 100 mg daily.

Participants not already taking metformin, not meeting referral criteria, and without contraindications were offered metformin initiation at 500 mg/day, with weekly titration to a maximum dose of 2 g/day.
In the case of an FBG or RBG < 4.4 mmol/l, the metformin dose was reduced by 500 mg/day.
text.formatted: In the case of an FBG or RBG < 4.4 mmol/l, the metformin dose was reduced by 500 mg/day.

text.text: Participants with an FBG > 8.0 mmol/l or an RBG > 9.9 mmol/l who reported good adherence to the maximum metformin dose were referred to the closest health facility for further management.

FGDs involving a total of 22 CHWs were conducted.
IDIs included two participants from Butha-Buthe district and two participants from Mokhotlong district.
The FGDs included eight participants in Butha-Buthe and ten participants in Mokhotlong.

Four participants had previous experience working as CHWs before the introduction of the digital system and were therefore able to reflect on differences between paper-based and digital workflows.Semi-structured interview guides explored experiences using the application, perceived benefits and challenges, training and support needs, usability, and the role of the application in supporting delivery of hypertension and diabetes care.
The guides were pilot-tested before data collection.

IDIs and FGDs were conducted in Sesotho by Motlalentoa Moruthoane, BSc Social Sciences, a male trained qualitative research assistant with previous experience conducting qualitative interviews and FGDs.
He was not involved in delivering the intervention or supervising participating CHWs.
Participants were informed of his role and the purpose of the qualitative study before data collection.
IDIs and FGDs were conducted at the training venue, with only the researcher and participants present, and lasted approximately 30-40 and 90-100 minutes, respectively.
Sessions were audio-recorded and translated into English during transcription.
No repeat interviews were conducted and no field notes were taken.
Transcripts were not returned to participants for comment or correction, and formal participant checking of the findings was not undertaken.
The semi-structured guide for IDIs and FGDs is available in Supporting Information (S2 Appendix).
The nested trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05596773, NCT05743387, and NCT05684055).
The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.
Additional information regarding the ethical, cultural, and scientific considerations specific to inclusivity in global research is included in the Supporting Information (S3 Checklist).

During the same period, 22 CHWs participated in the qualitative component through four IDIs and two FGDs.

All 103 CHWs had used the application for participant registration, screening, and diagnosis of hypertension and type 2 diabetes, while the 51 CHWs in intervention villages had additionally used it to support protocol-based treatment and longitudinal follow-up.

By the time of the evaluation, the application had been used to register 5283 households and 16297 participants, screen 8096 adults for hypertension and 6135 adults for type 2 diabetes, and support longitudinal care for 401 347 participants with hypertension and 60 participants with type 2 diabetes enrolled in the nested cluster-348 randomized trials.
The median age of participating CHWs was 32 years (IQR 28-39), 74 (72%) were 349 female, and 94 (91%) had completed at least secondary education.
